detail.abstract: We examine the interplay between monetary policy, bank risk-taking, and financial stability in a quantitative macroeconomic model with endogenous risk-taking by banks and systemic crises. Banks’ access to leverage depends on their charter value, which is itself affected by movements in the real interest rate. We find that permanent shifts in the long-term real interest rate have a significant impact on banks’ leverage and on their investments in systemically risky assets, while transitory movements have a more limited impact. We show that in the presence of systemic risk-taking, the systemic component of monetary policy faces a trade-off between price stability and financial stability. A moderate reaction to inflation deviations from the target is optimal, as it sustains banks’ equity value after financial crises. Seeking price stability reduces inflation volatility but leads to increased systemic risk-taking and more severe financial recessions. The optimal central bank policy combination involves an increase in regulatory bank capital requirements coupled with a moderate reaction of monetary policy to inflation.

title: Hard to Process: Atypical Firms and the Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns

detail.title: Hard to Process: Atypical Firms and the Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns
detail.abstract: Theories of limited attention predict that investors rely on typical patterns to navigate high-dimensional firm information, making atypical firms hard to process. To quantify this difficulty, we propose a data-driven measure of how atypical a firm's combination of characteristics is using an autoencoder (ATYP). The model learns the typical patterns that describe most firms, and ATYP aggregates the deviations those patterns cannot explain. Unlike measures of disclosure or organizational complexity, ATYP captures the processing difficulty of the underlying information. Empirically, we document that ATYP strongly predicts future returns. A decile portfolio that sells high-ATYP firms and buys low-ATYP firms earns 1.47% per month (equal-weighted) and 0.82% (value-weighted). The effect strengthens precisely where investor attention is low and arbitrage is limited, suggesting mispricing driven by limited information processing.

detail.title: Asset Risk and Bank Runs
detail.abstract: We analyze how the likelihood of bank-runs depends on bank asset risk. We introduce a Global Games-based bank-run model with balance sheet equity and risky assets. Elevated asset risk increases the probability of fundamentals-based bankruptcy and thereby may trigger bank-runs. However, elevated asset risk also induces higher returns in good states. These returns create additional loss absorption capacity and thereby lower the probability of non-fundamental bankruptcy. This in turn lowers the likelihood of bank-runs. The latter effect dominates when marginal benefits of capital are high (i.e., when banks are poorly capitalized).

detail.abstract: Recent developments in causal machine learning methods have made it easier to estimate flexible relationships between confounders, treatments and outcomes, making unconfoundedness assumptions in causal analysis more palatable. How successful are these approaches in recovering ground truth baselines? In this paper we analyze a new data sample including an experimental rollout of a new feature at a large technology company and a simultaneous sample of users who endogenously opted into the feature. We find that recovering ground truth causal effects is feasible-but only with careful modeling choices. Our results build on the observational causal literature beginning with LaLonde (1986), offering best practices for more credible treatment effect estimation in modern, high-dimensional datasets.

detail.abstract: In this study, we examine the relationship between housing hardship and parenting behaviors based on cross-sectional data from 777 low-income mothers with preschool children in Hong Kong. Drawing on the ecology of parenting framework, multiple linear regression models revealed indoor housing quality problems to be positively associated with aggressive parenting (measured by how often children were disciplined physically, or hit), after adjusting for the mothers’ and families’ socioeconomic conditions. Path analyses found that housing hardship increases maternal mental health problems, leading to aggressive parenting and residential dissatisfaction, further reducing the mothers’ engagement in daily parenting activities with their preschoolers. Our findings provide evidence of the effects of housing attributes and identify the salient influence of residential satisfaction on parenting styles in socioeconomically disadvantaged families. They also underscore the importance of addressing housing conditions in interventions aimed at improving parenting and, ultimately, child well-being.

title: Commercial Large Language Models in Clinical Practice: A Governance Framework for Use-Bound, Adaptive Integration

detail.abstract: Commercial large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are entering clinical workflows faster than any prior digital technology. Although developed as general-purpose conversational systems, their accessibility, fluency, and broad knowledge base have made them attractive to clinicians for tasks ranging from documentation and patient communication to diagnostic brainstorming. This rapid diffusion, however, has occurred largely outside formal institutional oversight, regulatory classification, or established accountability structures. As a result, a growing pattern of informal and unsanctioned use has emerged within healthcare systems. This paper argues that informal clinician adoption of LLMs is not merely a product of regulatory lag or individual experimentation, but reflects a deeper structural mismatch between how healthcare governance is designed to regulate diagnostic technologies and how general-purpose AI systems are built, updated, and deployed. Existing regulatory and institutional frameworks presuppose tools that are domain-specific, stable, versioned, and tied to clearly defined intended uses. Commercial LLMs violate each of these assumptions: they operate as open-domain generalists, evolve continuously through opaque updates, and lack clinically meaningful boundaries or validation pathways. Drawing on empirical evidence of emerging clinical use and established regulatory models such as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and the FDA's Predetermined Change Control Plan, this paper proposes an adapted governance framework for clinical LLM integration. The framework is structured around four principles: use-based boundaries, adaptive oversight, institution-centered responsibility, and distributed accountability. Together, these principles provide a foundation for governing general-purpose AI systems in ways that better align with the realities of clinical practice while preserving patient safety, professional accountability, and public trust.

detail.abstract: The evolving landscape of Islamic unity and approximation efforts requires a strategic and measurable approach to overcome sectarian differences and promote collaboration. This paper presents a comprehensive Key Performance Indicator (KPI) framework tailored to Islamic unity and approximation initiatives, addressing various dimensions such as educational programs, political collaboration, conflict resolution, and community engagement. Through a datadriven, KPI-based approach, Islamic organizations can systematically monitor and evaluate the progress of their approximation efforts, ensuring accountability, transparency, and long-term sustainability. The paper explores the significance of KPIs in fostering intersect collaboration, religious tolerance, and social cohesion across the global Islamic community. By showcasing best practices from successful initiatives and offering actionable insights, this research provides a roadmap for religious scholars, leaders, and institutions to enhance unity efforts using structured and strategic measurements. The findings highlight the potential of KPIs to transform traditional unity programs into impactful, scalable, and enduring initiatives that address contemporary challenges faced by the Islamic world.

title: Forward-Looking vs Reverse Geopolitical Stress Testing: What Boards Need to Know
affiliations: Central Bank of Bahrain

detail.title: Forward-Looking vs Reverse Geopolitical Stress Testing: What Boards Need to Know
detail.abstract: Geopolitical risk captures the possibility that wars, sanctions, cyberattacks, and abrupt shifts in international relations disrupt macro-financial conditions, impair asset values, and threaten cross-border business models. Banks traditionally manage this risk through country and sector limits, sanctions-sensitivity caps, and qualitative "red lines" in risk appetite frameworks, increasingly linked to heat maps, early-warning indicators, and stress-testing outputs. Forward-looking and reverse stress tests offer complementary ways to assess how such shocks could undermine capital, liquidity, and business-model viability. Forward-looking geopolitical stress tests start from "severe but plausible" scenarios, embedding deglobalization, trade fragmentation, energy shocks, and cyber risks into macro-financial paths that are then mapped into credit, market, operational, and funding metrics within ICAAP/ILAAP and regulatory stress tests. Reverse geopolitical stress tests invert this logic, starting from a defined failure outcome (for example, a 300-basis-point CET1 depletion or non-viability) and working backwards to identify the bank-specific geopolitical constellations and channels that could produce it, including second-round and feedback effects. Recent regulatory initiatives, such as the ECB's 2026 proposed thematic reverse stress test on geopolitical risk exemplifies this shift, requiring 110 directly supervised banks to design their own scenarios that meet an outcome constraint, integrate them into ICAAP, and use the results to strengthen internal stress-testing, governance, and risk data aggregation. While the exercise will not directly set Pillar 2 capital guidance, supervisors intend to use findings qualitatively in SREP to challenge business models, risk appetite, and recovery planning under radical geopolitical uncertainty. In this backdrop, the present paper discusses how banks should use both forward-looking and reverse stress testing to understand and manage geopolitical risk across capital, liquidity, and business-model dimensions. The paper stresses the role of stress tests in geopolitical risk assessment, looking at the synergies of conventional and reverse stress tests. It emphasizes the qualitative use of reverse stress test in SREP to test banks' governance, risk appetite, recovery planning, and internal stress-testing capabilities rather than to impose direct capital add-ons. It concludes that boards should treat forward-looking and reverse approaches as complementary tools that jointly inform risk appetite calibration, recovery options, strategic repositioning, and supervisory dialogue in an era of heightened geopolitical uncertainty.

title: Consumer xenocentrism in the majority world: Eco-anxiety mediates the effect of green consumption values and the fear of missing out on consumer xenocentrism in Ecuador

detail.title: Consumer xenocentrism in the majority world: Eco-anxiety mediates the effect of green consumption values and the fear of missing out on consumer xenocentrism in Ecuador
detail.abstract: As sustainability awareness grows, international companies have identified a trend of consumers seeking sustainable foreign products; therefore, they have integrated sustainable communication into their marketing strategies to convey these characteristics and influence consumer xenocentrism, which is the preference for foreign products. The use of sustainable communication can lead to eco-anxiety; hence, it becomes relevant to consider its influence on consumers who depict FOMO and green values. This study examines whether eco-anxiety mediates the effect of (a) the fear of missing out and (b) green consumption values on consumer xenocentrism. A total of 374 usable surveys were gathered from a sample of Ecuadorian consumers, and the study utilized Covariance-Structural Equation Modelling for data analysis. The findings indicate that eco-anxiety has an indirect effect across both these constructs, ultimately shaping consumer xenocentrism responses. This insight deepens our understanding of why consumers beyond Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) societies favor foreign products, emphasizing the role of sustainable communication in influencing consumer perceptions toward these products.

detail.abstract: The Contemporary Theory of Digitalization (CToD) seeks to explain digitalization not merely as the adoption of digital technologies, but as a comprehensive, systemic, and evolving transformation that reshapes how organizations function internally and how they interact with other organizations across global networks. CToD provides a logical and conceptual framework that helps organizations to understand, design, govern, and sustain digital transformation in a rapidly changing technological, economic, and social environment. The theory recognizes digitalization as a multidimensional phenomenon involving technology, people, processes, institutions, and power relations rather than a purely technical upgrade. The innovation of CToD lies in its three-level structure, which reflects increasing degrees of digital maturity and complexity. Level 1 is a foundational digital order, whereas Level 2 is an operational digitalization, and Level 3 is Digital Connectivity and Global Interaction. This layered approach allows scholars and practitioners to analyze digitalization systematically, identify weaknesses, and design targeted interventions. It also facilitates empirical testing and comparative analysis across sectors and jurisdictions.

detail.abstract: A persistent problem in corporate governance is the defining scope of the fiduciary and other duties of directors of public corporations, private companies, and other organisations that adopt a corporate form. Moreover, over the past three decades, public policy initiatives have sought to foster greater director accountability not just as a solution to the agency problem but also in aid of broader social goals. This push-and-pull of policy can confuse decision-making and for directors pose a version of the famous "trolley problem" in ethics, with the added complication that boards must decide on how to act collectively and not as individuals. This conceptual paper poses the question: Might the ethics of care-sometimes labelled "feminist ethics"-come to the rescue?

title: Uneven Modernization in the Muslim World

detail.title: Uneven Modernization in the Muslim World
detail.abstract: Modernization is a multidimensional process that enhances human welfare. The relative modernity levels of geographic units can be inferred from global migration patterns, which favor destinations offering opportunities deemed superior. On this basis, we introduce a migration-based "modernity index" and show that the Muslim World currently lags behind major recipient countries. The gap does not indicate stagnation. The Muslim World has been modernizing, though unevenly across time, regions, and sectors. Although existing research documents these variations, systematic analyses of differing paces and patterns of selective convergence remain scarce. This survey fills that gap by distinguishing among continuous, punctuated, and latent modernization trajectories and organizing the literature around four leading explanations for persistent developmental lags: collectivist attitudes, Islamic religious tenets, Islamic legal institutions, and colonial institutional legacies. The resulting framework highlights various sectoral contrasts, such as rapid progress in health and basic education alongside persistent deficits in political and religious liberties.

The analysis concludes that this condition constitutes a form of internal settler colonialism, fundamentally challenging the emancipatory promise of ethnic federalism and providing a crucial evidence-based model for scholars and policymakers analyzing engineered conflict, disenfranchisement, and institutional violence in the Horn of Africa and comparable contexts.

title: Value Stream Revolution: Reconstructing The Three Worlds of Enterprises (Organizations) --Theoretical Construction, Tool Derivation, and Case Validation Based on the Three-System Model of Creation, Realization, and Support

detail.title: Value Stream Revolution: Reconstructing The Three Worlds of Enterprises (Organizations) --Theoretical Construction, Tool Derivation, and Case Validation Based on the Three-System Model of Creation, Realization, and Support
detail.abstract: Traditional organizational management theories are facing a severe "crisis of explanatory power" as digital transformation accelerates and the global market environment increasingly presents the characteristics of VUCA (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity). This paper presents a paradigm reconfiguration based on "process dynamics" in response to the fundamental limitations of the "structural classification" paradigm in mainstream organizational theory-that is, the difficulty in effectively diagnosing chronic problems such as strategy-execution disconnection, departmental walls, and systemic synergy failure. This study disregards the traditional anatomical view of the enterprise as a static collection of functional departments (such as R&D, sales, finance), returns to the ontological origin of the existence of the enterprise, redefines it as a dynamic value stream system, regards the enterprise as a living entity centered around value generation and realization, and decomposes the core functions of the enterprise from this perspective as: Value generation, value realization, internal support, and systematic elaboration of the synergy logic driven by the "meta-mission". Based on this, this paper constructs the "value carrier Creation-value market Realization-internal Support" three-system model (C-M-S model). It reveals that the "C-M coupling degree" and the efficiency of the S system are key variables determining the performance and lifespan of the enterprise, and elaborates on the interaction mechanism of information flow, decision flow and incentive flow among the systems; Thirdly, a set of operationalized solutions from theory to practice was completed, and the diagnostic framework for the health and coupling of the three systems of the organization was developed. Through comparative analysis of actual cases, this framework not only reveals the pathology of "coupling mechanism breakdown" leading to decline, but also demonstrates that "coupling mechanism can be actively constructed and repaired" is at the core of successful organizational transformation. This study aims to provide a complete framework from theoretical construction, measurement blueprint to management intervention to drive organizational analysis from static structure to dynamic systems science.

title: Frequent Flyer Flagging - Proposed Model for Tracking Patterns of Lawyer Disciplinary Complaints

detail.title: Frequent Flyer Flagging - Proposed Model for Tracking Patterns of Lawyer Disciplinary Complaints

keywords: Model Rules For Lawyer Disciplinary Enforcement

detail.abstract:
The case of Thomas Girardi underscores the urgent need for reform in how grievances and patterns of misconduct are tracked. Over four decades, the California State Bar received and neglected more than 200 grievances against Girardi. It was only after his firm collapsed and criminal charges were filed that the Bar addressed the misconduct. Earlier intervention could have prevented the mishandling of eighteen million dollars and spared his clients from significant harm. This example of systemic oversight illustrates not only the imbalance of power between lawyers and clients, but also the tendency of disciplinary agencies to summarily dismiss most grievances at intake. 

Inspired by the Girardi case and subsequent California reform, this comment provides a novel approach to remedy the systemic weaknesses of the current discipline framework. It proposes implementing a “Frequent Flyer Flagging” system that uses complaint-pattern tracking to flag “frequent flyers” and provide timely notice of repeated misconduct. A frequent flyer is an attorney who receives an excessive number of grievances in a short period of time. Part I elaborates on the Girardi matter and its significance. Part II provides the background and explains the current regulatory framework. Part III recognizes and attempts to reconcile the competing interests of the public and the profession. In addition, this section recognizes the capabilities and limitations of a disciplinary intake office.

Part IV of this comment presents two models designed to identify and address patterns of excessive complaints. The models are fleshed out with options for phases, thresholds, and safeguards which can be tailored to complement each jurisdiction’s specific needs. Model A requires a flagged attorney to meet with disciplinary authorities to address the concerning pattern and to provide more information. If the board finds the prior dismissals were premature, it may reopen the files and resume the existing investigation process. Under Model B, subsequent complaints against a flagged attorney automatically proceed to investigation, bypassing the intake phase. The board should have discretion in deciding whether to advance the complaint or screen it out as a clearly frivolous matter. Both models preserve respondents’ due process rights while striking the proper balance between the parties’ interests.

By adopting a pattern-tracking system, disciplinary agencies can enhance accountability, protect the public, and restore confidence in the profession’s ability to self-regulate. To facilitate integration, this comment concludes by urging the ABA to conduct a comprehensive national review, issue updated reform recommendations, and to provide clearer guidance for intake and recordkeeping procedures.

title: Real Effects of Suppliers’ Environmental and Social Impact Disclosure
affiliations: Duke University and Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Real Effects of Suppliers’ Environmental and Social Impact Disclosure
detail.abstract: We study how the disclosure of suppliers' environmental and social impacts affects production choices and engagement levels of two competing firms. In our setting, the suppliers' production generates a negative impact that reduces the firms' cash flows. However, this impact is mitigated if the firms engage with their suppliers. When the firms have distinct suppliers, a firm's production choice and its engagement level are substitutes for those of the competing firm. Disclosure of the supplier's impact disciplines the firms and always increases the firms' surplus. In contrast, when the firms share a common supplier, the firms' production choices and engagement levels are either substitutes or complements. While some disclosure of the supplier's impact disciplines the firms and leads to a larger surplus than no disclosure, full disclosure is not always beneficial. In particular, the firms may be worse off with full disclosure than with partial disclosure as full disclosure may result in insufficient engagement due to the complementarity of the firms' engagement levels.

title: Buddhism and Economic Ethics: Integrating Spiritual Ideals with Material Reality
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: Buddhism and Economic Ethics: Integrating Spiritual Ideals with Material Reality
detail.abstract: This study examines the intersection of Buddhism and economic ethics, analyzing how Theravada and Mahayana traditions offer distinct yet complementary approaches to contemporary economic challenges. Employing a flexible integrated research methodology, the paper explores the philosophical foundations underlying Buddhist economic thought, tracing their origins to the Buddha's Middle Way, a balanced path that rejected both the extreme asceticism and materialistic hedonism prevalent in pre-Buddhist India. The fundamental distinction between the Theravada ideal of the Arahant (individual liberation) and the Mahayana ideal of the Bodhisattva (collective welfare) creates divergent economic philosophies: Theravada emphasizes personal ethical conduct, mindful consumption, and cautious engagement with wealth, while Mahayana promotes systemic transformation and the strategic use of wealth for societal benefit. Using Sri Lanka as a case study, the paper examines how a predominantly Theravada country displays economic behaviors increasingly aligned with Mahayana principles, creating a hybrid model that blends traditional spiritual values with modern capitalist practices. The analysis of the Sigalovada Sutta's fourfold division of wealth reveals both the enduring relevance and practical challenges of applying ancient Buddhist economic principles to contemporary issues including wealth inequality, consumerism, and globalization. The study concludes that integrating insights from both traditions offers pathways toward more compassionate, equitable, and sustainable economic systems.

title: Digital patient distribution as a disaster risk reduction measure in mass-casualty incidents Evidence from the Munich vehicle-ramming attack (2025)
affiliations: , , , ,  and

detail.title: Digital patient distribution as a disaster risk reduction measure in mass-casualty incidents Evidence from the Munich vehicle-ramming attack (2025)
detail.abstract: Urban mass-casualty incidents (MCIs), particularly those resulting from deliberate attacks, pose a significant challenge to disaster risk reduction due to the risk of cascading system failures, hospital overload, and delayed definitive care. Digital coordination systems are increasingly recognized as key enablers of system resilience in such high-impact, low-frequency events.This study analyzes the emergency medical response to a vehicle-ramming attack in Munich, Germany, on February 13, 2025, which resulted in 39 casualties, including two fatalities. Using retrospective operational data from a web-based mass-casualty coordination module integrated into the regional hospital capacity management system, we evaluated system performance with respect to communication speed, dynamic capacity adaptation, and patient distribution. Early activation of the digital coordination system by the integrated emergency dispatch center enabled transparent, real-time situational awareness and demand-oriented patient allocation. All critically injured patients were distributed across multiple hospitals within 19 minutes, preventing local overload and maintaining routine emergency care capacity citywide. Continuous digital feedback from hospitals allowed dynamic adjustment of resources throughout the incident.Beyond its operational benefits, the system provided comprehensive documentation that supported post-incident evaluation and organizational learning. Identified areas for improvement primarily concerned structured in-system communication between dispatch centers and hospitals.These findings highlight the role of digital patient distribution platforms as resilience-enhancing tools in urban disaster response. Integrating such systems into routine emergency workflows, combined with standardized preparation and training, represents an effective strategy for disaster risk reduction and the mitigation of secondary system failures during MCIs.

title: Advancing the Role of Temporal Experience in Relation to Workplace Thriving
affiliations: ,  and University of Technology Sydney

detail.title: Advancing the Role of Temporal Experience in Relation to Workplace Thriving

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Organizational Analysis, volume 34, issue 12, 2026[10.1108/IJOA-11-2024-5000]

detail.abstract: Purpose-This conceptual paper aims to explore organisational operating rhythms with a view to establishing a broader understanding of how they might be experienced in relation to wellbeing or thriving at both the organisational and individual levels. A model of operating rhythms is proposed, which integrates systems theory concepts alongside a new conception of individual and contextual enablers of thriving. Design/methodology/approach-A literature review is conducted on temporal workplace processes with the addition of wellbeing and thriving related terminology. This review was then used to synthesise perspectives from organisational analysis and positive organisational scholarship, providing new conceptual frameworks for understanding organisational temporal experiences in relation to thriving. Findings-Identifying limited prior research on temporal rhythms in organisations and the relationship to thriving and wellbeing, a conceptual link between these variables is developed to encourage and support further research in this area. This proposed model includes systems theory perspectives and suggests that workplace rhythms shape the flow of information, feedback, learning and interpersonal interaction, influencing the conditions that support thriving. Implications of this conceptualisation of organisational temporal experience provide potential approaches for use within organisational contexts. Originality/value-Two novel contributions are introduced. Firstly, a two-axis model that maps organisational rhythms along a continuum from strategic to operational (Y-axis) and intentional to emergent (X-axis). Secondly, the concept of a zone of interaction, where personal and contextual enablers of thriving intersect, is proposed as a lens to understand complex variables that, including operating rhythms, influence lived workplace experience at micro and macro levels.

title: Fiscal Costs and Implementation Feasibility of Minimum Price Support Policies: A Scenario Analysis
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University and  ICAR- National Institute of Biotic Stress Management

detail.title: Fiscal Costs and Implementation Feasibility of Minimum Price Support Policies: A Scenario Analysis
detail.abstract: For policymakers concerned with farm income stability and national food security, the Minimum Support Price (MSP) remains a critical instrument. However, some farmers organisations demand of extending assured physical procurement beyond paddy and wheat to all 23 MSP-notified crops would impose substantial fiscal and operational pressures. This paper quantifies the fiscal consequences of alternative MSP implementation pathways for the 2024-25 marketing year to inform evidence-based policy choices. We evaluate three policy options: (i) partial physical procurement, (ii) a mixed approach with partial Price Deficiency Payments (PDP), and (iii) universal PDP. Using crop-wise data on production, MSP, and modal market prices from Agmarknet and CEDA, we estimate farmer payouts, disposal revenues, and the resulting net fiscal burden under each scenario. If procurement is limited to 40% of paddy and wheat output and 20% of other crops, total farmer payouts are estimated at ₹4.67 lakh crore (about 1.4% of GDP), with a net fiscal burden ranging from ₹28,891 to ₹52,171 crore (0.09-0.16% of GDP) after accounting for disposal revenues. A partial PDP model, retaining procurement for paddy and wheat while extending PDP to 20% of output for other crops entails broadly similar fiscal costs but offers clear efficiency gains by sharply reducing storage, handling, and logistics requirements. Moving to a universal PDP slightly increases gross expenditure but eliminates inventory-related costs altogether, simplifying administration. Based on these estimates, we recommend a hybrid MSP framework: continue physical procurement for paddy and wheat to safeguard food security, while adopting PDP for other crops. This approach balances fiscal prudence with operational efficiency and aligns India's price support system with internationally accepted best practices, while still delivering effective income support to farmers.

title: The Concept of Economic Guarantees of Security and Targeted Sanctions Policy

detail.title: The Concept of Economic Guarantees of Security and Targeted Sanctions Policy

detail.abstract: Recent experience demonstrates that the effectiveness of sanctions policy depends less on the overall scale of economic damage and more on the precision and intensity of its impact on actual decision-makers and actors influencing decision-making processes. Broad-based sanctions frequently redistribute costs onto civilian populations, show weak correlation with changes in political behaviour, and contribute to the long-term institutional adaptation of sanctioned regimes. This preprint conceptualizes economic sanctions as a form of strategic communication and proposes a methodological shift from macroeconomic pressure to personalized and targeted interventions. Drawing on analytical tools developed in advertising and political marketing, the paper develops a typology of political regimes and corresponding sanctions-targeting strategies. It argues that increasing the effectiveness of sanctions requires identifying real centres of decision-making and tailoring instruments of influence to the specific political, economic, and industrial architecture of a regime, rather than expanding the scope of restrictions. Special attention is given to the role of credible threats of targeted sanctions as an independent deterrent factor capable of initiating internal resistance within sanctioned systems even prior to the formal imposition of restrictions. In this framework, targeted sanctions are interpreted as an integral element of a broader system of Economic Guarantees of Security, embedded within the architecture of conflict prevention and de-escalation.

title: Operator-Constrained Residual Connections: A Mathematical Framework for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Operator-Constrained Residual Connections: A Mathematical Framework for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
detail.abstract: We develop a general operator-theoretic framework for stable residual mixing in deep networks, formalizing operator-constrained residual connections as a design principle in which residual interactions are restricted to non-expansive matrix manifolds to guarantee depth-independent stability of the residual mixing path and to isolate stability conditions on the nonlinear blocks. Within this framework, we prove that the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices constitutes the canonical convex feasible set under nonnegativity and two-sided mass preservation, with operators that (i) preserve identity mappings exactly, (ii) are closed under composition, (iii) admit efficient differentiable projections, and (iv) induce mixing dynamics without spectral amplification. This paper provides the complete mathematical foundations for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), recently introduced by Xie et al. [2026] as a stabilization of the Hyper-Connections (HC) architecture proposed by Zhu et al. [2024]. We show that the doubly stochastic constraint enforces non-expansive residual dynamics, with operator norms uniformly bounded under composition and preserved under transposition. These properties yield provable control of gradient propagation, mitigating exploding and vanishing gradients arising from residual mixing under standard Lipschitz-type assumptions on the nonlinear blocks, while preserving a large (n-1) 2-dimensional mixing family. The constraint is implemented efficiently via Sinkhorn normalization, allowing implicit differentiation and seamless integration into transformer-style architectures without altering asymptotic complexity. Beyond explaining existing architectures, our operator-constrained perspective opens a systematic design space for future residual mechanisms governed by spectral theory rather than ad-hoc normalization, establishing manifold-constrained residual mixing as a unifying framework for stable deep network design.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has shifted from experimental technology to institutional force within regulated environments such as higher education and healthcare. AI systems now influence decisions affecting rights, safety, access, employment, and professional judgment, yet governance structures have not evolved to match this influence. AI is commonly introduced through procurement cycles, pilots, or vendor platforms without an explicit institutional decision that authorizes use, assigns accountability, or defines conditions for refusal. The result is governance failure rather than innovation risk: systems gain influence without permission, while responsibility remains diffuse until harm occurs.
